questions.stem: A business has a gross profit of $240,000 on revenue of $800,000. What is the gross profit margin?
whyNot: That divides revenue by gross profit and would not be a margin.
That misplaces the decimal point by a factor of ten.
That is gross profit subtracted from revenue, which is total cost of sales, not a margin.

questions.stem: Current assets are $180,000 and current liabilities are $120,000. What is the current ratio?
whyNot: That divides current liabilities by current assets, which is the wrong way round.
That is working capital in money terms, not a ratio.
The current ratio is expressed as a ratio, not a percentage.

questions.stem: Which of the following best defines gearing?
options: The proportion of a business's capital that is financed by long-term debt
The proportion of profit paid out as dividends
The speed at which inventory is sold
The return earned on each unit sold
questions.why: Gearing measures how far the business depends on borrowing rather than on equity.
whyNot: That is the dividend payout ratio.
That is inventory turnover.
That is a profit margin.

questions.stem: Which of the following best defines return on capital employed?
options: Operating profit expressed as a percentage of the capital invested in the business
Gross profit as a percentage of revenue
Cash held as a percentage of current liabilities
Profit after tax divided by the number of shares
questions.why: ROCE relates the profit earned to the money tied up in earning it, which is why it is treated as the primary measure of performance.
whyNot: That is the gross profit margin.
That is a liquidity measure, not a return.
That is earnings per share.

questions.stem: Operating profit is $90,000 and capital employed is $600,000. What is ROCE?
whyNot: That divides capital employed by operating profit, which is the wrong way round.
That subtracts one figure from the other, which is not a return.
That misplaces the decimal point by a factor of one hundred.

questions.stem: A business has a ROCE of 11% and can borrow at 7%. What is the key evaluative conclusion?
options: Borrowing to invest is worthwhile, because the return exceeds the cost of the finance
Borrowing should be avoided, because any debt increases risk to an unacceptable level
The two figures cannot be compared with each other
The business should repay all its debt immediately
questions.why: Comparing ROCE with the cost of borrowing is the central evaluation move in this topic: a return above the interest rate means debt adds value.
whyNot: Debt does raise risk, but a blanket rule ignores the fact that the return exceeds the cost.
They are directly comparable, and comparing them is exactly what the ratio is for.
Repaying debt that earns more than it costs would reduce returns to shareholders.

questions.stem: Which of the following best defines the payables days ratio?
options: The average number of days a business takes to pay its suppliers
The average number of days customers take to pay the business
The average number of days inventory is held before sale
The number of days of cash a business holds in reserve
questions.why: Payables days measures how long the business takes to settle its own trade debts.
whyNot: That is receivables days.
That is inventory turnover expressed in days.
That is not a standard ratio.

questions.stem: Receivables days rise from 35 to 62 while revenue is unchanged. What is the most likely concern?
options: Cash is being tied up in customers who are paying more slowly
The business has become more profitable
Inventory is being held for longer
Gearing has fallen
questions.why: Slower collection consumes cash without increasing sales, which creates a liquidity problem even though profit is unaffected.
whyNot: Collection speed does not change profit; it changes cash.
Inventory holding is measured by a different ratio.
Receivables days tell you nothing directly about the level of debt.

questions.stem: Why is a very high current ratio not necessarily a good sign?
options: Cash, inventory and receivables may be sitting idle instead of being invested productively
It means the business cannot pay its short-term debts
It always indicates that the business is loss-making
It means the business has too much long-term debt
questions.why: Liquidity has an opportunity cost, so an unusually high ratio may indicate poor use of resources rather than strength.
whyNot: A high ratio indicates it can comfortably pay short-term debts.
Liquidity and profitability are different things.
The current ratio concerns short-term items, not long-term debt.

questions.stem: A business has high gearing. Which pair of consequences is correct?
options: Greater risk from interest payments, and higher returns to shareholders if profits are strong
Lower risk from interest payments, and lower returns to shareholders
No effect on risk, and no effect on returns
Greater risk, and no possibility of higher returns
questions.why: Debt magnifies outcomes in both directions: fixed interest must be paid whatever happens, and any surplus above it belongs to the shareholders.
whyNot: High gearing raises risk rather than lowering it.
Gearing affects both the risk profile and the return to shareholders.
The potential for higher returns is exactly why businesses use debt.

questions.stem: Why must ratios be compared before they can be interpreted?
options: A single figure is meaningless without a trend, an industry benchmark or a competitor to compare with
Ratios are calculated differently every year
Ratios cannot be calculated from published statements
Ratios are only valid for businesses that export
questions.why: Comparison over time and against the sector is what turns a calculation into analysis, because normal levels differ enormously by industry.
whyNot: The formulas are consistent; the issue is the absence of a reference point.
Published statements are the standard source for ratio analysis.
Ratios apply to all businesses.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the strongest limitation of ratio analysis?
options: Ratios are based on historical financial data and ignore everything non-financial
Ratios require a computer to calculate
Ratios can only be calculated for listed companies
Ratios are not used by lenders
questions.why: They rest on past figures and say nothing about morale, brand, innovation or customer satisfaction, all of which drive future competitiveness.
whyNot: They are simple arithmetic.
Any business with financial statements can be analysed.
Lenders are among the heaviest users of ratio analysis.

questions.stem: Gross profit margin is stable but operating profit margin has fallen. What does this suggest?
options: Operating expenses have risen rather than the direct cost of sales
Selling prices have fallen sharply
Suppliers have raised their prices
Revenue has fallen
questions.why: The gap between the two margins is operating expenses, so if only the lower margin has fallen, overheads are the cause.
whyNot: A price fall would normally reduce the gross margin as well.
Higher supplier prices would appear in cost of sales and reduce the gross margin.
A fall in revenue alone would not necessarily change either margin.

questions.stem: Which of the following best defines inventory turnover?
options: How many times a business sells and replaces its inventory over a period
The total value of inventory held at the year end
The proportion of inventory that is damaged or unsold
The number of suppliers a business uses
questions.why: It measures how quickly stock moves, and it can also be expressed as the average number of days inventory is held.
whyNot: That is the closing inventory figure, which is an input to the ratio.
That is wastage, a separate operational measure.
Supplier numbers are unrelated to the ratio.

questions.stem: Why can two businesses in the same industry show non-comparable ratios?
options: They may use different accounting policies, for example in valuing assets
Ratios are calculated using different formulas in different businesses
One may publish statements and the other may not calculate profit
Ratios change meaning depending on the country's language
questions.why: Differences in accounting policy mean the underlying figures are not always measuring quite the same thing, so comparisons need care.
whyNot: The formulas are standard; the inputs are what differ.
Any trading business calculates profit.
Language does not affect the arithmetic or meaning of a ratio.

questions.stem: In a 20-mark question using ratios, which approach earns the most marks?
options: Calculate, compare with the previous year or the sector, explain the likely cause, then judge
Calculate as many ratios as possible and list the results
Describe what each ratio measures without using the figures given
State that the business is performing well because profit is positive
questions.why: The marks are in the interpretation and judgement, so each calculation needs a comparison, a cause and a conclusion.
whyNot: A list of unexplained numbers earns very few marks.
Describing formulas without applying them ignores the source.
Positive profit alone is not an assessment of performance.
